parentIntro: This week is about pulling numbers apart flexibly. 253 is 200 + 50 + 3 — but it's ALSO 240 + 13, or 100 + 153. Standard partitioning first, then the sneaky non-standard ways: that flexibility is what makes mental addition and subtraction possible later.
watchFor: Two classics: writing 200503 when she means 253 (gluing the parts together), and panicking at things like “14 tens” — if that happens, build it with blocks and trade ten sticks for a hundred square so she SEES 14 tens become 1 hundred and 4 tens.

demo.title: Pulling 253 apart
demo.say: Today we're going to pull a number to pieces, and put it back together in different ways. Watch what umma does with two hundred and fifty three.

steps.caption: 253 = 2 hundreds, 5 tens, 3 ones
steps.say: Here is two hundred and fifty three. Two hundreds, five tens, three ones.

steps.caption: the usual way
steps.say: We can write it as two hundred, plus fifty, plus three. That's the usual way to pull it apart.

steps.caption: 2 hundreds, 4 tens, 13 ones — still 253!
steps.say: Now watch this trick. I trade one ten for ten little ones. Two hundreds, four tens, and thirteen ones. Count it — it is STILL two hundred and fifty three!

steps.caption: a sneaky way — same number!
steps.say: So two hundred and fifty three is also two hundred and forty, plus thirteen. Same number, different pieces. That trick will help us with take-aways very soon.

weDo.model: Blocks or drawings: big square = 100, stick = 10, dot = 1. Build 174 first: one square, seven sticks, four dots.
steps: Ask: “What's the usual way to pull 174 apart?” (100 + 70 + 4 — write it down.)
Now the trick: take ONE stick and trade it for ten dots. Ask: “What have we got now?” (1 hundred, 6 tens, 14 ones.)
Ask her: “Is it still 174? How do you know?” — let her count to convince herself.

weDo.problem: Mystery number: “I have 3 hundreds and 15 tens. What number am I?”
weDo.model: Draw 3 big squares and 15 sticks. The magic move: circle ten of the sticks — ten tens make a hundred!
steps: Let her draw 3 squares and 15 sticks (count the sticks out loud together).
Ask: “Can we trade any sticks for a square?” (Ten sticks → one more square.)
Now count: 4 squares and 5 sticks. Ask: “So what number was I?”
If she enjoys it, fire back: “I have 2 hundreds and 13 tens — beat that one!” (330)
